content: A birth cohort study identified a significant relationship between changes in conditional weight from age 11 to adulthood and elevated total cholesterol levels. Regarding height, two studies presented conflicting findings: one demonstrated an association between childhood height and adult cholesterol levels, while the other found no such link. A significant association was observed between childhood waist circumference, the sum of skinfolds at age 9, and increased total cholesterol levels in adulthood. Additionally, the Bogalusa Heart Study reported a positive correlation between childhood triceps skinfold thickness and adult cholesterol levels. However, the Northern Finland Birth Cohort of 1966 found no association between the age of adiposity rebound and higher cholesterol levels in adulthood. Positive associations were found between childhood BMI and triglyceride levels in adulthood in studies from the Terneuzen Birth Cohort, Bogalusa Heart Study, and the 1958 British Birth Cohort. Conversely, no association was observed between infant BMI and triglyceride levels in adolescence or adulthood in the Vulnerable Windows Cohort Study and the Northern Finland Birth Cohort of 1966. The Newcastle Thousand Families Cohort Study reported an inverse relationship between childhood BMI and adult triglyceride levels. The Bogalusa Heart Study also demonstrated a significant association between adolescent weight status, BMI changes, and adult triglyceride levels. The Northern Finland Birth Cohort of 1966 and the New Delhi Birth Cohort Study reported that a BMI percentile above the 90th and changes in conditional BMI from age 2 to adulthood increased the risk of high triglyceride levels in adulthood. Weight during infancy, childhood, and adolescence was also studied for its association with adult triglyceride levels. No association was found between infant weight and adult triglyceride levels in the Vulnerable Windows Cohort Study. The New Delhi Birth Cohort Study found a significant association between conditional weight from birth to adulthood and triglyceride levels in adulthood. Height during infancy and childhood showed no association with adult triglyceride levels in the Vulnerable Windows Cohort Study. Rapid increases in waist circumference during childhood were associated with higher odds of elevated triglyceride levels in adolescence, as reported by ALSPAC and the NHLBI study. Skinfold thickness in childhood was not significantly associated with adolescent triglyceride levels in the NHLBI study, but a positive correlation was observed between skinfold thickness from ages 2 to 17 and triglyceride levels in adolescence. An inverse relationship between childhood BMI and adult LDL levels was reported by the Newcastle Thousand Families Cohort Study. BMI at adiposity rebound was not associated with adult LDL levels when adjusted for socioeconomic and maternal factors. Rapid increases in BMI during childhood were linked to higher odds of elevated LDL levels in adolescence, as observed in the ALSPAC study. Two studies reported significant associations between childhood waist circumference and rapid increases in waist circumference with the highest LDL levels in adulthood. Childhood skinfold thickness was positively associated with adolescent and adult LDL levels in the Bogalusa Heart Study and NHLBI study. Two reports from the Bogalusa Heart Study showed an inverse association between childhood BMI and adult HDL levels, adjusted for race, age, and sex. The Northern Finland Birth Cohort Study reported no significant association between childhood BMI and adult HDL levels. A weak inverse relationship in females and a weak positive relationship in males were observed between childhood BMI and adult HDL levels when adjusted for BMI at age 50. Changes in conditional BMI from age 11 to adulthood were significantly associated with lower adult HDL levels. The Northern Finland Birth Cohort of 1966 found no association between childhood adiposity rebound and adult HDL levels. The 1958 British Birth Cohort reported a negative association between BMI changes from ages 7 to 16 and adult HDL levels. Four studies examined the impact of childhood weight on adult HDL levels. The New Delhi Birth Cohort observed a significant association between changes in conditional weight from age 11 to adulthood and lower adult HDL levels. The Vulnerable Windows Cohort found an association between weight increases from ages 2 to 11 and lower HDL levels at age 11. Three studies examined the relationship between height and adult HDL levels. The Vulnerable Windows Cohort found no association between birth height and HDL levels at age 11. Subjects with peak height velocity greater than 8 cm/year did not have an increased risk of lower HDL levels in adulthood. Two studies examined the impact of childhood waist circumference on adult HDL levels. Both ALSPAC and NHLBI reported that rapid increases in waist circumference during childhood were associated with higher odds of developing low HDL levels in adolescence. Childhood triceps skinfold thickness was negatively correlated with adult HDL levels when adjusted for race, age, and sex. The NHLBI study found a significant association between childhood skinfold thickness and decreased HDL levels in adolescence.
